title: Kansas Fields; the drum as the heartbeat and African origin of percussion
summary: Jones talks of Kansas Fields, then says the drummer is the heart of the band, that the drum came from Africa, and what was lost by segregation.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: No question about that. I'd just like to mention, we got to J. C. Heard. We got to mention, what are some of the few guys that came in our band, into

Cab Calloway's band, and Cozy leaving and going to CBS and J. C. Heard taking his place and doing such an admirable job and really making it so smooth and easy to work with. I was there. You know we had an influx of young drummers that came in - Kansas Fields. You remember Fields? Kansas Fields came in. I can't exactly recite the order when Kansas Fields came through. You remember Kansas?
Of course I do. He went to Paris.
I think he's in Chicago now, right?

Yes. Kansas, when he came back from Europe, went to my friend Oliver, O. J. That's where he stayed. Now you see, Milt, we must remember this. Since I took to the drums I found out that the drummer was the key. The drummer was the key; this was the heartbeat of the body of music. Now we all have individual lives to live. A lot of us were not allowed the privilege to play with whom we wanted to play with. We had to do what we had to do. That's the one instrument that has nothing to do with race, color, or creed, which everybody knows the first instrument is the drum. Where did it come from? It came from Africa. So you forget about that, so whatever they did superficial with that, it doesn't mean anything. But when you go into various parts of the world, when it comes to percussion, everybody realized that it came from Africa. They can't deny that, I don't care where you go, 400 years ago, 500

years ago, this year, any time. But when the peoples that sit down in percussion, when they do these different things they have to do what they have to do. Now when peoples get out here and get just a little name they place them in a certain position and it's the drum that is the key. You see, he's got to sit there like the heart of the body and ho, not used but utilized. As I reiterated before, could you imagine what would have happened had a Gene Krupa or a Buddy Rich or a Shelly Manne had had a chance to play with a Cab Calloway, a Jimmy Lunceford, a Lucky Millinder or what have you. Which. comes to mind one little drummer - I'm always had little children out here. This is a little drummer. Well, let me see, Shelly Manne - they used to keep me up at night because Shelly Manne's father was with Radio City and - oh, we lost so much with our backward ignorant intelligence. That's what I call it, ignorant intelligence. Instead of them leaving us alone and going and doing their nine to five they had to interject and to try to tell us what to do.
Hi, I'm glad you mentioned him.
